newsitem.title: CYPRUS: UK foreign minister in Cyprus to boost talks.
newsitem.headline: UK foreign minister in Cyprus to boost talks.

text.p: British Foreign Minister Malcolm Rifkind on Sunday arrived in Cyprus to add weight to efforts to persuade the Greek and Turkish communities to start peace talks but warned against expecting a quick breakthrough.

"I have no illusions about the difficulties involved... we are all realistic and know progress won't happen overnight," said Rifkind, the first British Foreign Secretary to visit the divided eastern Mediterranean island for 30 years.

He said the international community was increasingly concerned by an upsurge in violence over the last six months in which four people were killed in or near the buffer zone separating Turkish and Greek Cypriots.

"At a time when the Cold War is over, the Berlin Wall has fallen and apartheid is no more, surely it is not unrealistic that this small beautiful island can find a peace and justice acceptable to all," he told reporters on arrival in Cyprus.
The United Nations has been trying without success for decades to broker a settlement and the international community has come to the conclusion that the Cyprus problem cannot be allowed to fester.

U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali said last week that the situation on the island was the worst since Turkish troops invaded the northern third in 1974 after a coup on the island engineered by the military regime then ruling Greece.
"It is of the utmost importance that we find a workable solution...we've lived with the consequences far too long," Cypriot Foreign Minister Alecos Michaelides told reporters.
"I am optimistic that 1997 might be the year for Cyprus."
Rifkind, speaking earlier on board his plane, said the international community could not afford to dawdle.

"As we've seen over the last few months, the lack of a political settlement means that even the smallest incident has led to serious loss of life. The situation is not stable -- it could descend into serious conflict," he said.

The Turkish Cypriots, whose self-declared state is only recognised by Ankara, have around 35,000 Turkish and Turkish Cypriots troops. The Cypriot National Guard has 11,500 troops but recently acquired 77 Russian and French battle tanks.
Both Turkey and Greece have defence pacts with their respective communities on the island.
"Given the small size of Cyprus and its population, the military presence is clearly disproportionate," Rifkind said.
British officials are optimistic that Cyprus President Glafcos Clerides and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash will hold face-to-face talks in the next six months.
Rifkind, however, said it would be wrong to expect too much from a visit that was part of a long-term process.
"One doesn't achieve dramatic results in two days. I hope this visit will give added momentum to a process which has already started and will encourage a resumption of political dialogue," he said.

One possible key to talks is Cyprus's desire to open talks on European Union membership and Rifkind said it would be much easier for the island to gain entry to the EU if a political settlement was reached first.
Rifkind said all of Cyprus stood to gain huge economic benefits if the decades-old inter-communal tension could be resolved, but acknowledged the international community could only do so much.
"I have no doubt there will only be progress if both sides want progress. The outside world can only take the process forwards if the political will exists on the island."
Rifkind was due to hold a working dinner with Michaelides later on Sunday. He will hold separate talks with Clerides and Denktash on Monday.
